clips.text_en_b2: Bitcoin versus gold: if you could hold only one asset for the next ten years, which would you choose, and what makes your case stronger than the alternative? This question surfaced on /biz/ today, but most anons responded with jokes and memes rather than a serious analysis. Gold is backed by central banks, whereas Bitcoin ultimately relies on market consensus. Although technical and fundamental analysis may offer clues, neither can provide a definitive answer. Genuine arguments are welcome.
clips.text_en_c1: Were you compelled to liquidate every alternative position and hold nothing but a single asset for the coming decade, Bitcoin or gold would secure your allegiance, and on what grounds does that conviction outweigh the rival case? The thread surfaced on /biz/ this morning and, predictably, devolved into the usual avalanche of memes and unserious posting, though a handful of anons have been making what look like substantive arguments, weighing central-bank endorsement against decentralised consensus, scarcity narratives against network effects. Neither technical analysis nor fundamental astrology, whichever one takes seriously, resolves the dilemma. Genuine reasoning, however flawed, would be a welcome departure from the noise.
clips.text_en_c2: A question surfaced on /biz/ that genuinely merits deliberation: if one were compelled to hold a single asset for the coming decade, should it be Bitcoin or gold, and what substantive reasoning underpins that preference? Most respondents, predictably, resorted to facile shitposting rather than rigorous analysis. Gold benefits from centuries of institutional trust, central-bank endorsement, and an entrenched role as a monetary anchor; Bitcoin, by contrast, derives its value entirely from decentralised consensus and cryptographic scarcity. Neither technical analysis nor astrological speculation offers a definitive verdict, yet the inquiry itself remains intellectually compelling, particularly for those already allocating capital across both instruments and seeking a more principled framework for conviction.

clips.text_en_b2: On September 9, 2026, roughly 319 million additional SpaceX shares will become eligible for sale. The release marks the 90th trading day since the company’s IPO and its third major lockup expiration. Although the shares may not all enter the market immediately, traders will be watching whether the increased supply puts pressure on TSLA or affects prop firms holding large positions.
clips.text_en_c1: On the ninth of September 2026, approximately 319 million additional SpaceX shares — equivalent to roughly seven percent of the baseline pool or about two and a half percent of total shares outstanding — will become eligible for sale, marking the ninetieth trading day since the IPO. This constitutes the third major lockup expiry, and prop desks are reportedly scrambling to model the overhang, since insider liquidations of this magnitude have historically exerted downward pressure even on names with strong fundamentals. Whether Tesla absorbs collateral damage depends on correlation and sentiment, but the trading desks I have spoken to are bracing themselves.
clips.text_en_c2: On 9 September 2026, approximately 319 million SpaceX shares will become eligible for resale, representing some 2.4 percent of total shares outstanding and roughly 7 percent of the baseline pool. This event, the third major lockup expiry since the company's IPO, coincides with the customary ninetieth trading day after the offering, a calendar inflection that institutional investors monitor with considerable vigilance. The implications extend well beyond SpaceX itself; should the float generate downward pressure, adjacent equities such as Tesla may experience correlated volatility, given the high-beta exposure favoured by prop-trading desks. Whether insider conviction or mere liquidity arithmetic will dominate remains an open question, one that market participants would do well to dissect in advance.

clips.text_en_b2: Have you noticed how often people insist that ChatGPT Plus or other paid models are the only AI products worth trying? They argue that users cannot understand their capabilities until they have experienced the paid tier, which is allegedly far more capable. clips.text_en_c1: Have you encountered that particular breed of post in which the author insists, with almost evangelical fervour, that anyone who has not sampled the paid tier of frontier models simply cannot appreciate their capabilities, and that those who try them will find them terrifying? The premise deserves scrutiny, because the open-weights ecosystem — Kimi, GLM, Qwen among others — now delivers something close to ninety percent of that performance at perhaps ten percent of the cost. I personally passed a licensing exam largely through Qwen-assisted study, which rather undermines the notion that meaningful capability remains exclusively behind a paywall.
clips.text_en_c2: A recurring strain of commentary insists that only paid-tier large language models deliver genuinely capable output, yet such assertions betray a certain incuriosity about the contemporary open-weight landscape. Models such as Kimi, Qwen, and GLM routinely achieve performance within striking distance of flagship offerings, often at a tenth of the subscription cost, a disparity that renders the premium tier something of a luxury rather than a necessity. For budget-constrained users, myself included, these alternatives have proven entirely serviceable for cognitively demanding tasks; professional licensure preparation, for instance, has been substantially supported by Qwen without recourse to a paid plan. The presumption that capability scales linearly with expenditure deserves more rigorous scrutiny than its proponents typically provide.

clips.text_en_b2: Twenty-one U.S. banks reportedly plan to launch a joint stablecoin, which some see as the real purpose behind Trump’s stablecoin bill. Before long, critics expect a flood of branded digital currencies, including Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, Tesla Coin, X Coin, and Bank Coin. The argument is that private companies and financial institutions are taking over the American economy. If hundreds of such currencies enter circulation, they could weaken the dollar’s position. What would that mean for Bitcoin, gold, and the wider financial system?
clips.text_en_c1: Twenty-one American banks are reportedly preparing to roll out a joint stablecoin, a development that many now regard as the genuine underlying rationale for the Trump administration's stablecoin legislation. Once the regulatory door swings open, expect a cascade of corporate issuers — Apple Coin, Google Coin, Microsoft Coin, Tesla Coin, X Coin, Bank Coin — flooding the financial plumbing with hundreds of distinct digital instruments. Whether such saturation entrenches dollar hegemony or dilutes it remains contested, though the implications for Bitcoin and gold, which thrive on monetary distrust, could prove considerable.
clips.text_en_c2: Twenty-one American banks have coalesced around the prospect of issuing a jointly administered stablecoin, a development whose significance transcends the immediate technical innovation and gestures toward something more structural. Critics contend that the underlying legislation, ostensibly championed by the Trump administration, effectively privatises the architecture of digital dollar circulation, ceding monetary infrastructure to consortia whose interests may not align with broader public welfare. The anticipated proliferation of corporate-issued tokens, ranging from Apple Coin and Microsoft Coin to X Coin and Bank Coin, portends a fragmented settlement landscape in which the dollar's primacy could erode not through external challenge but through internal dilution. Should that scenario materialise, Bitcoin and gold may yet find themselves reassessed as alternative stores of value.

Should any responders wish to contribute, I would be grateful for spoiler-free reflections on early job selections, as I am presently weighing the relative merits of several disciplines. clips.text_en_c1: How frequently does one actually witness a 405-pound bench press in a commercial gym setting, because by any honest accounting it remains a vanishingly rare event? Anons across the thread offered that in the typical big-box facility you might see such a number attempted perhaps once every several months, whereas dedicated powerlifting gyms tend to produce one almost every session, given the clientele. Several veterans remarked that pressing 405 raw, without the assistance of a suit or wraps, represents a lifetime milestone for natural lifters. Tagging my training partner who has yet to lock down a single-plate overhead press, may we both reach that threshold by thirty-five.
clips.text_en_c2: The sighting of a 405-pound bench press in a commercial gym remains, statistically speaking, a genuinely rare occurrence, perhaps once every several months in a typical setting, whereas serious powerlifting facilities witness such feats on an almost quotidian basis. For drug-free lifters, pressing 405 raw constitutes a benchmark widely regarded as a lifetime milestone, one that demarcates the merely dedicated from the genuinely committed. I find myself, candidly, nowhere near that threshold; my own pressing numbers remain modest, and the prospect of attaining such strength by thirty-five feels ambitious rather than implausible. Nonetheless, the discipline required to pursue such a goal confers benefits that transcend the numerical outcome itself.
